Bank Churn Prediction

Problem Statement¶

Context¶

Businesses like banks which provide service have to worry about problem of 'Customer Churn' i.e. customers leaving and joining another service provider. It is important to understand which aspects of the service influence a customer's decision in this regard. Management can concentrate efforts on improvement of service, keeping in mind these priorities.

Objective¶

You as a Data scientist with the bank need to build a neural network based classifier that can determine whether a customer will leave the bank or not in the next 6 months.

Data Dictionary¶

  • CustomerId: Unique ID which is assigned to each customer

  • Surname: Last name of the customer

  • CreditScore: It defines the credit history of the customer.

  • Geography: A customer’s location

  • Gender: It defines the Gender of the customer

  • Age: Age of the customer

  • Tenure: Number of years for which the customer has been with the bank

  • NumOfProducts: refers to the number of products that a customer has purchased through the bank.

  • Balance: Account balance

  • HasCrCard: It is a categorical variable which decides whether the customer has credit card or not.

  • EstimatedSalary: Estimated salary

  • isActiveMember: Is is a categorical variable which decides whether the customer is active member of the bank or not ( Active member in the sense, using bank products regularly, making transactions etc )

  • Exited : whether or not the customer left the bank within six month. It can take two values ** 0=No ( Customer did not leave the bank ) ** 1=Yes ( Customer left the bank )

Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Univariate Analysis¶

The below functions need to be defined to carry out the Exploratory Data Analysis.¶

In [ ]:
# function to plot a boxplot and a histogram along the same scale.


def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(12, 7), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (12,7))
    kde: whether to show the density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,  # Number of rows of the subplot grid= 2
        sharex=True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize=figsize,
    )  # creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, x=feature, ax=ax_box2, showmeans=True, color="violet"
    )  # boxplot will be created and a star will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins, palette="winter"
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2
    )  # For histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--"
    )  # Add mean to the histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-"
    )  # Add median to the histogram
In [ ]:
# function to create labeled barplots


def labeled_barplot(data, feature, perc=False, n=None):
    """
    Barplot with percentage at the top

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    perc: whether to display percentages instead of count (default is False)
    n: displays the top n category levels (default is None, i.e., display all levels)
    """

    total = len(data[feature])  # length of the column
    count = data[feature].nunique()
    if n is None:
        plt.figure(figsize=(count + 1, 5))
    else:
        plt.figure(figsize=(n + 1, 5))

    plt.xticks(rotation=90, fontsize=15)
    ax = sns.countplot(
        data=data,
        x=feature,
        palette="Paired",
        order=data[feature].value_counts().index[:n].sort_values(),
    )

    for p in ax.patches:
        if perc == True:
            label = "{:.1f}%".format(
                100 * p.get_height() / total
            )  # percentage of each class of the category
        else:
            label = p.get_height()  # count of each level of the category

        x = p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2  # width of the plot
        y = p.get_height()  # height of the plot

        ax.annotate(
            label,
            (x, y),
            ha="center",
            va="center",
            size=12,
            xytext=(0, 5),
            textcoords="offset points",
        )  # annotate the percentage

    plt.show()  # show the plot
In [ ]:
# Code to create histogram and boxplot on CreditScore, Age , Balance and Estimated Salary

def call_histogram_boxplot(data, features):
    for feature in features:
        histogram_boxplot(data, feature)

features = ['CreditScore', 'Age', 'Balance', 'EstimatedSalary']
call_histogram_boxplot(data, features)

Observations

  • Credit score is left skewed. 50% percentile of population lies between a score 600 and 710.
  • Age is heavily right skewed. Majority of the customers are between the age of 30 - 40. This is an area which can be looked into. Further investigation may be needed to check if the churn factor is more in the other age groups.
  • Balance has a normal distribution between 100K - 150K.
  • There are 3500 (about 1/3) customers with 0 balance. This is an area which needs to be looked into deeply may be some offers for these group of customers so that they invest more in bank.
  • Salary is also equally distributed.
In [ ]:
# recursively calling the function labeled_barplot for Exited,Geography,Gender,Tenure,NumOfProducts,HasCrCard,isActiveMember

def call_labeled_barplot(data, features):
    for feature in features:
        labeled_barplot(data, feature)

features_to_plot = ['Exited', 'Geography', 'Gender', 'Tenure', 'NumOfProducts', 'HasCrCard', 'IsActiveMember']
call_labeled_barplot(data, features_to_plot)

Observations

  • 80% of the customer has not exited. So the data is imbalanced.
  • 50% of customers are from France.
  • There are more male customers than female customers.
  • There is a sudden drop in customers who have tenures = 10 years. This area needs to be investigated why long term customers are churning. Retention offers can be targeted towards who are in this group so that they dont churn. Most of the customers have 1 or 2 products. Extremely low number of customers has more than 2 products. This area can also be explored , if customers can be upsell with more products.
  • About 1/3 of the customers dont have credit card. Can this area be explored as well and customers are offered to take credit cards.
  • 4849 members are not active members. This dormant group could potentially churn. Bank should target this group so that they get more engaged.

# function to plot stacked bar chart


def stacked_barplot(data, predictor, target):
    """
    Print the category counts and plot a stacked bar chart

    data: dataframe
    predictor: independent variable
    target: target variable
    """
    count = data[predictor].nunique()
    sorter = data[target].value_counts().index[-1]
    tab1 = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], margins=True).sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    print(tab1)
    print("-" * 120)
    tab = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], normalize="index").sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    tab.plot(kind="bar", stacked=True, figsize=(count + 1, 5))
    plt.legend(
        loc="lower left",
        frameon=False,
    )
    plt.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(1, 1))
    plt.show()

# recursively call sns.boxplot to create plots where Exited against CreditScore,Age,Tenure,Balance,NumOfProducts,EstimatedSalary

def recursive_boxplot(data, features, target='Exited', i=0):
    if i < len(features):
        plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
        sns.boxplot(x=target, y=features[i], data=data)
        plt.title(f'Boxplot of {features[i]} vs. {target}')
        plt.show()
        recursive_boxplot(data, features, target, i + 1)

features = ['CreditScore', 'Age', 'Tenure', 'Balance', 'NumOfProducts', 'EstimatedSalary']
recursive_boxplot(data, features)

Observations

  • Germany has the highest percentage of churned customer. German part of the banks business would need more attention and investigation.
  • Female customers are less but they have churned more than male counterparts. This is an area that needs research , maybe bank should role female friendly programs to retain female customers.
  • Active members are less likely to churn. Bank should focus on inactive members and attract them to use the products more.
  • Credit score range is almost same between churn and non-churn so this may not be a strong feature.
  • Age group of churned customers are more than age group of non-churned customers. Non churned customers have significant outliers.
  • 75% of Customers who have churned have a longer tenure in the bank than 75% of non churned customers. This is something that needs investigation because bank is loosing long time customers.
  • Distribution of Number of products and Estimated salary are almost same for churned and non-churned customer. They may not be a good feature.

Model Building¶

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

creating a function for plotting the confusion matrix

In [14]:
def make_confusion_matrix(actual_targets, predicted_targets):
    """
    To plot the confusion_matrix with percentages

    actual_targets: actual target (dependent) variable values
    predicted_targets: predicted target (dependent) variable values
    """
    cm = confusion_matrix(actual_targets, predicted_targets)
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(cm.shape[0], cm.shape[1])

    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="")
    plt.ylabel("True label")
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")

Let's create two blank dataframes that will store the recall values for all the models we build.

In [15]:
# Recall is considered because cost of false nagtive is high.
train_metric_df = pd.DataFrame(columns=["recall"])
valid_metric_df = pd.DataFrame(columns=["recall"])

NOTE - We are considering RECALL as our important parameter because we need minimum False negative. In other words if model predicts a customer wont churn but the customer churns then it would be loss of business for bank. we want to avoid such scenarios.

Loss function

In [22]:
#Plotting Train Loss vs Validation Loss
plt.plot(history_0.history['loss'])
plt.plot(history_0.history['val_loss'])
plt.title('model loss')
plt.ylabel('Loss')
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.legend(['train', 'validation'], loc='upper left')
plt.show()

Observations

  • Both the training and validation loss decrease over epochs, indicating that the model is learning and improving during training.
  • The validation loss follows the training loss closely, suggesting that the model generalizes well to unseen data and is not overfitting.
  • The loss curves appear to be flattening as the number of epochs increases, indicating that the model is reaching convergence.

Recall

In [23]:
#Plotting Train recall vs Validation recall
plt.plot(history_0.history['recall'])
plt.plot(history_0.history['val_recall'])
plt.title('model recall')
plt.ylabel('Recall')
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.legend(['train', 'validation'], loc='upper left')
plt.show()

Observations

  • The recall values for both training and validation quickly drop to near zero after the first few epochs and remain there for most of the training process. This indicates that the model is struggling to correctly identify positive instances.
  • Likely cause could be the imbalance in the dataset used.

Neural Network with Adam Optimizer¶

backend.clear_session()
#Fixing the seed for random number generators so that we can ensure we receive the same output everytime
np.random.seed(2)
random.seed(2)
tf.random.set_seed(2)
In [32]:
#Initializing the neural network
model_1 = Sequential()
#adding a input layer
model_1.add(Dense(64,activation='relu',input_dim = X_train.shape[1]))
#adding a hidden layer
model_1.add(Dense(32,activation='relu'))
#adding a output layer with the required number of neurons and relu as activation function
model_1.add(Dense(1, activation = 'sigmoid'))
In [33]:
#Using Adam as the optimizer.
optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.Adam()
In [34]:
metric = keras.metrics.Recall()
In [35]:
# Complete the code to compile the model with binary cross entropy as loss function and recall as the metric
model_1.compile(loss='binary_crossentropy',optimizer=optimizer,metrics=[metric])

Loss function

In [38]:
#Plotting Train Loss vs Validation Loss
plt.plot(history_1.history['loss'])
plt.plot(history_1.history['val_loss'])
plt.title('model loss')
plt.ylabel('Loss')
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.legend(['train', 'validation'], loc='upper left')
plt.show()

Observations

  • The training loss continues to decrease steadily, while the validation loss initially decreases but then starts increasing after a certain point (around epoch 10-15). This suggests that the model is overfitting to the training data.

Recall

In [39]:
#Plotting Train recall vs Validation recall
plt.plot(history_1.history['recall'])
plt.plot(history_1.history['val_recall'])
plt.title('model recall')
plt.ylabel('Recall')
plt.xlabel('Epoch')
plt.legend(['train', 'validation'], loc='upper left')
plt.show()

Observations

  • Recall is still low.On training though it increased with EPOCH but still always remained < .5
  • Validation recall is worse than that.

Neural Network with Adam Optimizer and Dropout¶

backend.clear_session()

np.random.seed(2)
random.seed(2)
tf.random.set_seed(2)
In [48]:
#Initializing the neural network
model_2 = Sequential()
#Adding the input layer with 32 neurons and relu as activation function
model_2.add(Dense(32,activation='relu',input_dim = X_train.shape[1]))
model_2.add(Dropout(0.2))
model_2.add(Dense(16,activation='relu'))
model_2.add(Dense(8,activation='relu'))
model_2.add(Dropout(0.1))
model_2.add(Dense(4,activation='relu'))
model_2.add(Dense(1, activation = 'sigmoid'))
In [49]:
optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.Adam()
In [50]:
metric = keras.metrics.Recall()
In [51]:
model_2.compile(loss='binary_crossentropy',optimizer=optimizer,metrics=[metric])

Observation

  • Model's performance across training validation set seems to be at par.
  • Reducing the neurons and also adding dropout actually helped in reducing overfitting.

Neural Network with Balanced Data (by applying SMOTE) and SGD Optimizer¶

It is observed that the model's had tendency of overfitting. One of the main reason for that is imbalanced data. Trying SMOTE to reduce the imbalance.

In [67]:
sm  = SMOTE(random_state=42)
X_train_smote, y_train_smote= sm.fit_resample(X_train, y_train)
print('After UpSampling, the shape of train_X: {}'.format(X_train_smote.shape))
print('After UpSampling, the shape of train_y: {} \n'.format(y_train_smote.shape))

After UpSampling, the shape of train_X: (9554, 11)
After UpSampling, the shape of train_y: (9554,)

Observations

  • Major improvement of Recall score on validation set.
  • SMOTE has helped overcome the imbalance in data. Due to which model is now behaving more generically.
  • Recall score across training and validation set is almost same. So model is behaving in a genaralized way.
  • Loss also reduced smoothly.

Neural Network with Balanced Data (by applying SMOTE) and Adam Optimizer¶

Observations

  • Major improvement of Recall score on validation set than just ADAM optimizer and Adam optimizer with dropout.
  • SMOTE has helped overcome the imbalance in data. Due to which model is now behaving more generically.
  • Recall score across training and validation set is almost same. So model is behaving in a genaralized way.

Neural Network with Balanced Data (by applying SMOTE), Adam Optimizer, and Dropout¶

Observation

  • model_3 (SMOTE with SGD) performed extremely well on test data.
  • Only 97 instances of false negative which is within the acceptable limit.

Actionable Insights and Business Recommendations¶

  • Bank can use the neural network with Balanced Data (by applying SMOTE) and SGD Optimizer as its model to predict customer churn. If the model decides that a customer may churn. Then special attention needs to be given to those customers.
  • 75% of customers who have churned had a longer tenure with the bank compared to 75% of non-churned customers. This warrants investigation, as the bank is losing long-term customers.
  • Active members have a lower likelihood of churning. The bank should prioritize engaging inactive members and encouraging them to use its products more.
  • Germany has the highest percentage of churned customers. The bank should focus on this region and conduct a thorough investigation to understand the underlying causes.
  • There are 3,500 customers (approximately one-third) with a zero balance. This issue requires deeper analysis, and the bank should consider offering incentives to encourage these customers to invest more.

Power Ahead
